title: B2B Ecommerce Platform Selection 2026: An APAC Buyer Guide
summary: A practical B2B ecommerce platform selection 2026 framework for APAC: evaluation criteria, real pricing, a weighted scoring matrix, and a six-week process.
body_markdown:
**Quick Answer:** B2B ecommerce platform selection in 2026 hinges on three things: whether your pricing logic fits the platform natively, how mature its ERP connector is, and 36-month total cost. Score candidates on your own price book — not vendor demo data — before shortlisting.


---


Gartner's forecast that 80% of B2B sales interactions between suppliers and buyers will occur in digital channels by 2025 has aged into a floor, not a ceiling. The companies I speak with across Hong Kong, Singapore and Taiwan are no longer asking whether to put their dealer or wholesale channel online. They are asking which platform survives contact with their ERP, their multi-currency price books, and their credit terms. That is what makes B2B ecommerce platform selection 2026 a different exercise from the one most vendor comparison pages describe: the feature checklists converged two years ago, and the differentiation moved into integration surface, pricing model, and who maintains the thing in year three.

## Start With Order Shape, Not Feature Lists


Before you look at a single vendor, document how orders actually enter your business today. Not how you wish they did. In most APAC B2B operations I've reviewed, the real order flow looks like this: a WhatsApp message or email from a long-standing buyer, manually keyed into an ERP by a customer service rep, priced from a spreadsheet of negotiated rates, shipped against credit terms that exist nowhere in a system.


That is not a platform problem. That is a data problem, and it determines which platform category you can realistically deploy.


Four questions produce more selection signal than any feature matrix:


**How many distinct price lists exist?** If the answer is under 20 customer groups with percentage-off-list logic, mainstream SaaS handles it. If you have per-SKU negotiated pricing for 400 dealers with volume breaks and contract expiry dates, your pricing engine lives in the ERP and the storefront is a read layer.


**What is the order line count distribution?** A 2,000-line replenishment order behaves nothing like a 12-line order. Carts, checkout timeouts, and tax calculation all break differently at that volume. Ask vendors for their documented line-item ceiling, in writing.


**Where does inventory truth live?** Multi-warehouse allocation across HK, Shenzhen and a Singapore 3PL is the single most common source of post-launch pain. If your ERP cannot expose available-to-promise per location via API, no platform fixes that.


**Who approves what?** Buyer-side approval chains — requisition, budget holder, finance sign-off — are the feature B2B buyers in regulated sectors actually ask for, and the one most mid-market platforms implement shallowly.


## The Three Architecture Paths Worth Evaluating


Almost every serious shortlist in 2026 collapses into three shapes. Understand what each one is actually optimising for.


### Path 1: SaaS-First (Shopify Plus, BigCommerce B2B Edition, SHOPLINE)


Shopify's B2B functionality — company profiles, catalogue-level price lists, payment terms, and B2B-specific checkout — moved from a bolt-on to native platform capability and now ships with Plus. Shopify reported in its Q4 2024 shareholder letter that B2B GMV grew 145% year over year, which tells you where the product investment is going.


What SaaS-first buys you: launch in 8–16 weeks, no infrastructure ownership, a functioning app marketplace, and predictable platform spend. What it costs you: pricing logic must fit the platform's model. Shopify's B2B catalogues handle fixed prices and percentage adjustments per company location well. They do not natively handle contract-expiry-aware tiered pricing with ERP as the source of truth — you build that with Shopify Functions, metafields, or a middleware pricing service.


For APAC specifically, Shopify's weak point remains localised B2B payment and invoicing practice. Net-30 against a credit limit tracked in SAP, with a local-format invoice for Taiwan GUI compliance or Indonesia e-faktur, is integration work in every case.


### Path 2: ERP-Integrated Commerce (OroCommerce, SAP Commerce Cloud, Adobe Commerce B2B)


This path treats the ERP as the commerce brain. Pricing, credit, inventory, and customer hierarchy stay in SAP, Oracle, Microsoft Dynamics 365 Business Central, or a regional system like Sage 300 or Yonyou. The storefront reads and writes.


OroCommerce and Adobe Commerce B2B both ship native B2B primitives — corporate account hierarchies, quote-to-order workflows, shared shopping lists, requisition approvals — that you would otherwise build. Adobe Commerce in particular carries genuine depth here, but Adobe's own documentation makes clear that B2B features require the Commerce (not Open Source) edition, and Adobe moved its pricing to a revenue-share-adjacent model that scales uncomfortably for high-GMV, low-margin distribution businesses.


The honest trade-off: ERP-integrated commerce gives you pricing correctness at the cost of release velocity. Every merchandising change that touches price or availability now has an ERP dependency.


### Path 3: Composable / Headless (commercetools, Shopify Hydrogen, Medusa, Saleor)


Composable means you assemble commerce from APIs — a commerce engine, a separate CMS, a separate search provider, a separate PIM — and own the frontend. MACH Alliance members push this hard, and for a reason: it is genuinely the right answer when you have multiple brands, multiple regions, and multiple front ends (web, dealer portal, sales-rep app, marketplace feeds) sharing one catalogue.


It is the wrong answer when you have one storefront and no in-house engineering. Composable shifts cost from licence to labour. You are now permanently staffing a frontend team, a middleware team, and whoever maintains the four SaaS contracts underneath.


I'd put the threshold roughly here: composable earns its keep above US$30–50M in digital channel revenue, or when a single catalogue must serve three or more distinct consumption surfaces. Below that, you are paying enterprise architecture costs for mid-market needs.

## Seven Evaluation Criteria That Actually Separate Platforms


Score every shortlisted vendor against these. Weightings follow in the next section.


**1. Pricing engine depth.** Can the platform express your real price book natively, or does it require middleware? Ask for a demo using *your* pricing rules, not theirs. This single test eliminates half of most shortlists.


**2. ERP integration maturity.** Not "we have an API" — ask for the named connector, its maintainer, and its release cadence. A vendor-maintained SAP connector is a different risk profile from a partner-built one that stops being updated.


**3. Multi-entity and multi-currency handling.** APAC groups typically run separate legal entities per market. Can one platform instance serve HK, SG and AU entities with separate tax treatment, or do you need three instances? Shopify Markets handles currency and tax presentment well; it does not solve separate statutory invoicing.


**4. B2B workflow natives.** Quote-to-order, requisition approval, buyer hierarchies, reorder from past orders, CSV/bulk upload, and sales-rep order-on-behalf. Count how many require apps versus core.


**5. Performance at catalogue scale.** 50,000+ SKUs with customer-specific pricing is a search and caching problem. Ask what their largest live B2B catalogue is and whether you can speak to that merchant.


**6. Total cost of ownership over 36 months.** Licence plus implementation plus annual maintenance plus the apps. Not year-one list price.


**7. Regional operational fit.** Payment methods (FPS in Hong Kong, PayNow in Singapore, DuitNow in Malaysia, VietQR in Vietnam), logistics connectors, local tax compliance, and whether support operates in your timezone. A US-centric vendor with 9am–5pm Pacific support is a real constraint for a Taipei operations team.


## What These Platforms Actually Cost in 2026


Published numbers, with the caveat that enterprise deals are negotiated and most vendors will not publish their real floor.


### Platform licence


- **Shopify Plus** : from US$2,300/month on a three-year term, or US$2,500/month monthly, per Shopify's published pricing. Variable platform fee applies above revenue thresholds — typically 0.2–0.4% of GMV for high-volume merchants, which matters enormously for distribution businesses running thin margins on high turnover. Run the maths at your actual GMV before assuming the headline price.
- **BigCommerce Enterprise** : quote-based, commonly landing in the US$1,500–4,000/month range depending on order volume; BigCommerce publishes tiers up to Pro at US$299/month and quotes above that.
- **Adobe Commerce** : licence scales with Gross Merchandise Value; public estimates place entry around US$40,000–60,000/year with large deployments well into six figures. Adobe does not publish list pricing.
- **commercetools** : subscription-based, quote-only. Industry reporting puts entry-level enterprise agreements above US$100,000/year.
- **OroCommerce** : Enterprise Edition is quote-based; OroCommerce also publishes a free Community Edition, which is genuinely useful for proof-of-concept work.
- **SHOPLINE** : significantly lower entry point for APAC-headquartered merchants, with regional payment and logistics integrations that Western platforms charge apps for. Weaker on deep B2B pricing logic.


### Implementation


This is where budgets break. Rough bands from APAC systems-integration work:


- Shopify Plus B2B with a single ERP integration: US$60,000–180,000
- Adobe Commerce B2B, multi-entity: US$250,000–800,000
- commercetools composable build, multi-brand: US$400,000–1.5M+
- OroCommerce with SAP integration: US$150,000–500,000


The integration layer typically consumes 35–50% of implementation budget in ERP-connected B2B projects. If a vendor's proposal allocates 10% to integration, they have not understood your order flow.


### Ongoing


Budget 15–25% of implementation cost annually for maintenance, platform upgrades, and the inevitable second-wave features. For composable, add dedicated engineering headcount — that is the honest line item nobody puts in the business case.

## A Scoring Framework You Can Run in a Week


Use a weighted 1–5 score per criterion. Weightings below reflect what I've seen actually predict project outcomes for APAC distribution and manufacturing businesses. Adjust, but adjust deliberately.


### Weightings


- ERP integration maturity — **25%**
- Pricing engine depth — **20%**
- Total 36-month cost of ownership — **15%**
- B2B workflow natives — **15%**
- Multi-entity / multi-currency — **10%**
- Performance at catalogue scale — **10%**
- Regional operational fit — **5%**


### How to score honestly


Score 5 only where the capability is native and you have seen it demonstrated on your data. Score 3 where it requires a documented, vendor-supported extension. Score 1 where it requires custom development with no reference implementation.


The discipline that makes this work: **run the demo on your own price book and your own order file.** Export 200 real SKUs, five real customer price lists, and one genuinely large historical order. Hand that to each vendor as a precondition for shortlisting. Vendors who decline have told you something.


### Reading your scores


If SaaS-first scores within 15% of ERP-integrated on your weighted total, take SaaS-first — the lower implementation risk and faster time-to-revenue is worth more than the marginal capability. If composable only wins on criteria weighted under 10%, it is not winning.


## Is B2B Business Still Good in 2026?


Short answer: structurally yes, cyclically mixed. Digital Commerce 360 has consistently reported that US B2B ecommerce site and marketplace sales continue to outpace overall B2B sales growth, and McKinsey's B2B Pulse research has repeatedly found that B2B buyers now use roughly ten channels in their purchasing journey, up from five in 2016.


What has changed is who captures the margin. Buyers increasingly expect self-service price visibility, which removes the information asymmetry that supported some distributor margins. The companies doing well are the ones using the platform to reduce cost-to-serve — order entry automation, self-service reorder, rep time redirected to accounts that need it — rather than treating the storefront as a new acquisition channel.


For Asia-Pacific specifically, cross-border B2B is where the growth sits. A manufacturer in Vietnam or a components supplier in Taiwan selling directly to European or US buyers now has platform options that didn't exist cheaply five years ago. That cuts both ways: Western brands increasingly run their APAC distribution from a Singapore or Hong Kong entity precisely because the regional payment, logistics and tax integration work is easier to staff here.

## What Are the Top B2B Ecommerce Trends Shaping 2026?


**Agentic buying.** Procurement systems and AI agents that place orders programmatically need machine-readable catalogues, not pretty PDPs. Practically, that means structured product data, stable SKU identifiers, and a real product API. If your PIM is a spreadsheet, you are not ready.


**Embedded finance.** Net terms underwritten by third parties — Balance, Hokodo, and regional equivalents — let you offer credit without carrying the risk on your balance sheet. Check which of these actually operate in your markets; APAC coverage is thinner than the US.


**Marketplace and multi-surface selling.** One catalogue feeding your own storefront, a dealer portal, Alibaba.com, and Amazon Business simultaneously. This is the single strongest argument for a headless product data layer even if your storefront stays on SaaS.


**Consolidation of the mid-market.** Shopify and BigCommerce have both pushed native B2B capability down-market aggressively, which has squeezed the mid-tier specialist vendors. Expect fewer independent options at the US$50K–150K implementation band by 2027.


## A Pattern From the Field


One engagement shape I see often: a manufacturer selling through a 200-plus dealer network across several APAC markets, running pricing out of an on-premise ERP, with dealers ordering by email. The instinct is to buy the platform with the deepest native B2B feature set. The better move is usually to fix the data contract first — get the ERP exposing clean price, stock and credit via API — then pick the thinnest storefront that consumes it.


When the pricing service is properly abstracted, the storefront becomes a replaceable component. That is worth more over five years than any single platform's feature depth, because it means your next replatform is a frontend project rather than a rebuild.

## How to Evaluate: A Six-Week Sequence


If you take one process away from this guide, take this. B2B ecommerce platform selection 2026 rewards structured evaluation over vendor charisma.


**Week 1 — Document order reality.** Pull 90 days of real orders. Count line distribution, price-list variants, approval paths, and how many orders were manually keyed. Quantify the manual handling cost. That number is your business case.


**Week 2 — Audit the ERP's API surface.** Can it expose price, available-to-promise by location, customer credit status, and accept order writes? Get your ERP partner to confirm in writing which endpoints exist and their rate limits. This determines your architecture more than any vendor decision.


**Week 3 — Shortlist three, not eight.** One per architecture path. Send each the same data pack: 200 SKUs, five price lists, one large order, your entity structure.


**Week 4 — Demo on your data.** Watch them price your SKUs for your customers. Note what required custom work. Note how they answered when they couldn't do something — the honest ones are easier to work with for the next three years.


**Week 5 — Score and cost.** Apply the weighted framework. Build the 36-month TCO including implementation, apps, maintenance and internal headcount. Compare against the Week 1 manual handling cost.


**Week 6 — Reference checks in your region.** Speak to a live merchant of similar complexity, ideally in APAC. Ask specifically what broke after launch and how long the integration took versus the estimate.


The companies that get this right treat platform selection as an operations decision with a software component, not a software decision. The storefront is the easy part. The price book, the credit terms, and the inventory truth are the project.
